asBirthCard.p: This one has nothing to do with your signs. It comes from the date you were born, every digit added up and brought down until it lands on a Major, and yours came down to two. Two is the first number that has company. The Magician before it is one, a man with his arm in the air making something happen on his own. By two there's a second thing in the room, so there's a gap between them, and the question of what's going on in that gap. That's where The High Priestess sits. Have a look at her, parked between a dark pillar and a light one, hands still, in no hurry at all. The card belongs to the Moon, and the Moon doesn't make its own light, it takes the Sun's and gives it back changed, and it goes through phases. Your version of two works much the same way. You take things in first and let them turn over, and only later does anything come back out.

Mostly it looks like knowing things a bit early. You're at a family dinner and you've clocked that your cousin's marriage is in trouble before the main course, from the way she passes the salt. In a meeting you're watching the person who hasn't said anything, and you're usually right about why. When a text comes in that needs a real answer you'll often leave it for a day, and it isn't rudeness, you just can't reply properly until you know what you think. A Sunday with nothing planned doesn't bother you at all. It's probably where you do your best thinking, on the couch, apparently doing nothing. People sometimes read all this as shyness. It's closer to attention, and you've had it since you were small.

The obvious gift is intuition, and you've heard that one. The less obvious one is that you can hold a pair of opposites at once without needing to settle them. Two friends fall out and both of them end up ringing you, because neither feels you've picked a side, and you genuinely haven't. You can see that your mother was hard on you and also that she was doing her best, and sit with both for years without it tearing you in half. Most people need a verdict quickly. You're comfortable in the waiting room, and that makes you very good at timing. You tend to know when a thing is ready to be said, and when saying it early would just waste it.

The trouble with seeing things early is that it can become a reason never to move. You knew the restructure was coming at work. You'd felt it for months. And you still didn't update your CV, because knowing felt like enough, like you'd already dealt with it somehow. Two people carry a quiet pride in being the one who saw it, and that pride can turn into a private sort of I-told-you-so that nobody else ever hears. The other thing is that waiting for the right moment is a lovely skill until it turns into waiting forever. Some doors don't open twice. If you notice you've been sitting on a decision for longer than a season, it's usually fear by then, and it's fine to call it that.

When something goes badly wrong, a loss, a work crisis, a friend turning on you, your first move is to go very quiet. You stop answering messages. You sleep more, or you don't sleep and lie there sorting it. From the outside it can look like you're coping beautifully. A week later you're usually still in there, and this is the part that's hard on the people around you, because they can tell something's wrong and have no way in. A partner starts guessing, and guessing wrong. What helps is giving one person one sentence. Just the headline, 'my dad's test results came back and I'm scared', so they don't have to read your face for clues. Then take the time alone, but put an edge on it. A few days is plenty, and tell someone roughly when you'll be back.

Being so good at reading people has a catch in love, which is that you tend to expect the same back. You notice when your partner's tired before they've said a word, so part of you feels they ought to notice when you are, and when they don't it lands as a small betrayal you never mention. It isn't one. Most people simply can't do what you do, and it's not a lack of love. The other pattern is falling for what's hidden in someone, the potential, the person you can sense under the difficult one, and staying for that version long after the actual one has shown you who they are. Say what you need in plain words, even though it feels clumsy. It gets easier with practice.

You're suited to any job where people hand you something private and trust you to hold it. Counselling, nursing, HR, research, editing, legal work, the night shift in a hospital, the archive nobody else wants to sort. You're good with information that's half there, a patient who can't say what's wrong, a manuscript that's nearly working, a client who's clearly not telling you everything. The frustration tends to be that your best work is invisible. You spotted the problem before it became one, so there's nothing to show for it, and the louder colleague who fixed a crisis gets the credit. It's worth getting into the habit of writing things down and sending the email. 'Flagging this now in case it grows.' It puts your name on what you saw.

At twenty a lot of two people don't trust any of this. You get a strong feeling about a flatmate or a boyfriend or a job, someone louder talks you out of it, and it turns out you were right, and this happens a few times before it sinks in. By the mid-thirties there's usually enough of a track record that you stop asking permission from your own hunches. You start acting on them sooner, and relationships tend to get better around then because you're choosing more carefully. The fifties often bring people to your door. Younger colleagues, nieces, neighbours, all wanting to know what you think, and the work at that stage is learning to actually tell them, out loud, instead of just knowing it privately.

Next time you're in a group, a dinner, a team meeting, a family barbecue, say the thing you've noticed within the first half hour. Keep it light. 'Is everyone else feeling a bit tense in here, or is it me?' or 'You seem quieter than usual, all good?' You'll feel the urge to hold onto it and see if you're right. Let yourself be wrong in public once. Then see what the room does with it.
